title: Chapter 15 — That Religious Belief Sometimes Turns The Thoughts Of The Americans To Immaterial Pleasures
paragraphs: In the United States, on the seventh day of every week, the nation’s commercial and working life seems to stop. All noise ceases. A deep stillness, or rather the solemn calm of meditation, takes the place of the week’s turmoil, and the soul comes back into possession of itself and reflects on itself. On this day the marketplaces stand empty. Every member of the community goes to church with his children, and there he hears language that seems strange and ill suited to his ears. He is told of the countless evils caused by pride and covetousness. He is reminded that he must restrain his desires, that finer pleasures belong to virtue alone, and that true happiness goes with it. When he returns home, he does not reach for the ledgers of his trade; he opens the book of Holy Scripture. There he finds sublime or moving descriptions of the greatness and goodness of the Creator, of the infinite magnificence of God’s handiwork, of the lofty destiny of man, of his duties, and of his immortal privileges. In this way the American at times steals an hour from himself. Setting aside for a while the petty passions that stir his life and the passing interests that absorb it, he wanders at once into an ideal world where everything is great, eternal, and pure.

In another part of this work I tried to point out the causes to which the maintenance of the Americans’ political institutions is owed, and religion appeared to be one of the most prominent of them. Here I am treating the Americans as individuals, and I observe once more that religion is no less useful to each citizen than to the state as a whole. By their practice the Americans show that they feel keenly how necessary it is to give democratic communities their morality by means of religion. What they think of themselves in this respect is a truth of which every democratic nation ought to be thoroughly convinced.

I do not doubt that a people’s social and political constitution inclines them toward a certain belief and certain tastes, which then flourish among them without difficulty. The same causes may turn a people away from certain opinions and propensities, without any deliberate effort on their part and, as it were, without their being clearly aware of it. The whole art of the legislator lies in discerning these natural inclinations of communities of men in advance, so as to know whether they should be helped or whether it may be necessary to check them. For the legislator’s duties differ from one age to another. Only the goal toward which the human race ought always to be moving stays fixed; the means of reaching it must constantly change.

Had I been born in an aristocratic age, in the midst of a nation where the inherited wealth of some and the hopeless poverty of others alike turn men away from the idea of improving their condition, and hold the soul, as it were, in a torpor fixed on the contemplation of another world, I should then wish to rouse that people to a sense of their needs. I should look for quicker and easier means of satisfying the new desires I had awakened. I should direct the most vigorous efforts of the human mind to physical pursuits, and try to spur it on to promote the well-being of man. If some men were excessively stirred up to chase after riches and showed an immoderate liking for physical gratifications, I should not be alarmed; these particular symptoms would soon be lost in the general character of the people.

The legislators of democracies have other concerns to attend to. Give democratic nations education and freedom, and then leave them alone. They will soon learn to draw from this world every benefit it can offer. They will improve each of the useful arts and make life more comfortable, more convenient, and easier day by day. Their social condition pushes them naturally in this direction, and I do not fear that they will slow down.

But while man takes pleasure in this honest and lawful pursuit of his well-being, there is reason to fear that he may in the end lose the use of his noblest faculties, and that while he is busy improving everything around him, he may at length degrade himself. The danger lies here, and only here. The legislators of democracies, and all the virtuous and educated men who live in them, should therefore make it their constant aim to raise the souls of their fellow citizens and keep them lifted toward heaven. All who care about the future of democratic society must unite, and all must make joint and continual efforts to spread the love of the infinite, a sense of greatness, and a love of pleasures that are not of this earth. If, among the opinions of a democratic people, there are any of those pernicious theories that teach that everything perishes with the body, then let the men who profess such theories be marked out as that people’s natural enemies.

The materialists offend me in many respects. I consider their doctrines pernicious, and their arrogance disgusts me. If their system could be of any use to man, it would seem to be by giving him a modest opinion of himself. But these reasoners show that it does not; and when they think they have said enough to prove that they are brutes, they appear as proud as if they had proved that they are gods. Materialism is a dangerous disease of the human mind among all nations, but it is especially to be feared among a democratic people, because it blends easily with the vice that is most familiar to the heart in those circumstances. Democracy encourages a taste for physical gratification. If this taste becomes excessive, it soon leads men to believe that everything is only matter; and materialism, in turn, hurries them back with mad impatience to those same pleasures. Such is the fatal circle in which democratic nations are driven around. It would be well if they saw the danger and held back.

Most religions are simply general, simple, and practical ways of teaching men the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. That is the greatest benefit a democratic people gets from its belief, and so belief is more necessary to such a people than to any other. Therefore, when a religion has sunk its roots deep into a democracy, take care not to disturb them. Watch over it instead, as the most precious legacy of aristocratic ages. Do not try to replace men’s old religious opinions with new ones, for in passing from one faith to another the soul may be left for a while stripped of all belief, and the love of physical gratifications could then grow in it and fill it entirely.

The doctrine of metempsychosis is certainly no more rational than materialism. Nevertheless, if a democracy absolutely had to choose one of the two, I would not hesitate to say that the community would run less risk of being brutalized by believing that the soul of man will pass into the carcass of a hog than by believing that the soul of man is nothing at all. Belief in a supersensual and immortal principle, joined for a time to matter, is so indispensable to man’s greatness that its effects are striking even when it is not joined to the doctrine of future reward and punishment, and when it holds no more than that, after death, the divine principle in man is absorbed into the Deity or passes into the frame of some other creature to animate it. Men with so imperfect a belief will still regard the body as the secondary and inferior part of their nature. They will despise it even while they yield to its influence. Meanwhile they have a natural respect and secret admiration for the immaterial part of man, even though they sometimes refuse to submit to its rule. That is enough to give a lofty cast to their opinions and tastes, and to make them tend, without any self-interested motive and almost by impulse, toward pure feelings and elevated thoughts.

It is not certain that Socrates and his followers held very fixed opinions about what would happen to man in the hereafter. But the one point of belief on which they were resolved — that the soul has nothing in common with the body and outlives it — was enough to give Platonic philosophy the sublime aspiration that distinguishes it. Plato’s works make clear that many philosophical writers, his predecessors or contemporaries, professed materialism. Their writings have not come down to us, or have reached us only in fragments. The same has happened in almost every age: the greater part of the most famous minds in literature adhere to the doctrines of a supersensual philosophy. The instinct and taste of the human race sustain those doctrines. They often save them in spite of men themselves, and raise the names of their defenders above the tide of time. It must not be supposed, then, that at any period or under any political condition, the passion for physical gratifications, and the opinions that this passion brings in its train, can ever satisfy a whole people. The heart of man is cast on a larger mold. It can hold at once a taste for the possessions of earth and a love of those of heaven. At times it may seem to cling devotedly to one, but it will never go long without thinking of the other.

It is easy to see that spiritual opinions are especially important in democratic ages, but it is not easy to say by what means those who govern democratic nations can make them prevail. I do not believe in the prosperity of official philosophies, any more than in their durability. As for state religions, I have always held that, although they may sometimes serve the interests of political power for a moment, they always become fatal to the Church sooner or later. Nor do I agree with those who maintain that, to raise religion in the eyes of the people and make them honor its spiritual doctrines, it is desirable to give her ministers, indirectly, a political influence that the laws deny them. I am so keenly aware of the almost inevitable dangers that threaten religious belief whenever the clergy take part in public affairs, and so convinced that Christianity must be maintained at any cost in the midst of modern democracies, that I would rather confine the priesthood within the sanctuary than let them step beyond it.

What means, then, remain in the hands of the constituted authorities to bring men back to spiritual opinions, or to hold them fast to the religion that suggests those opinions? My answer will damage me in the eyes of politicians. I believe the only effective means that governments can use to have the doctrine of the immortality of the soul properly respected is always to act as if they believed it themselves. And I think that only by strict conformity to religious morality in great affairs can they hope to teach the community at large to know it, to love it, and to observe it in the smaller concerns of life.
